missions.title: Mathematical Challenges
missions.subtitle: Choose your difficulty level and test your knowledge

ch1.title: 🍎 Apples on the farm
ch1.description: The farm has 24 apples. 3/4 of the harvest has been picked. How many apples have been picked?
ch1.hint: Multiply the total (24) by the fraction (3/4): 24 × 3/4

ch2.title: 🍕 Sharing pizza
ch2.description: You have 1/2 of a pizza and your friend gives you 1/4 more. How much pizza do you have now?
ch2.hint: Find a common denominator: 1/2 = 2/4, then add.

ch3.title: 🎂 Birthday cake
ch3.description: A cake is cut into 8 pieces. If you eat 3, what fraction of the cake have you eaten?
ch3.hint: The fraction is: pieces eaten / total number of pieces
ch3.success: Well done! You have eaten 3/8 of the cake.
ch3.error: Divide the pieces eaten by the total.

ch4.title: ⏰ Study time
ch4.description: You studied for 45 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes. What fraction of an hour did you study?
ch4.hint: 45/60 can be simplified by dividing both by 15.

ch5.title: 🏡 The farm's land
ch5.description: The land measures 12 km². 1/3 is used for apple trees, 1/4 for the vegetable garden and the rest for pasture. What fraction is pasture?
ch5.success: Exactly! 1 - 1/3 - 1/4 = 5/12 of the land is pasture.

ch6.title: 🧁 Cake recipe
ch6.description: The recipe needs 2/3 of a cup of sugar for 4 people. How much sugar for 10 people?
ch6.hint: Work out for 1 person: (2/3) ÷ 4. Then multiply by 10.
ch6.success: Perfect! You need 5/3 cups (1 and 2/3) of sugar.

ch7.title: 📊 Percentages and fractions
ch7.description: 60% of the students passed. What is it as a simplified fraction?
ch7.hint: 60% = 60/100. Simplify by dividing by the GCD.

ch8.title: 🏃 Relay race
ch8.description: A runner completes 3/7 of the route in 15 minutes. How many minutes will it take in total?

ch9.title: 🏀 The Bouncing Ball
ch9.description: A ball bounces back to 2/3 of its previous height. If on the second bounce it reaches 8 metres, from what height was it dropped?
ch9.hint: Work backwards. If the last height is 8m, the one before was 8 ÷ (2/3). Do this twice.
ch9.error: Remember: Height × (2/3) × (2/3) = 8. Solve for the Height.

ch10.title: 🚰 Taps and tanks
ch10.description: One tap takes 2 hours to fill a tank, and another takes 6 hours. How many minutes will both take together?
ch10.hint: In one hour, one fills 1/2 and the other 1/6. Add both.
ch10.success: Well done! 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3 fill per hour. So they take 3/2 hours = 90 minutes.
ch10.error: Add up what they fill per hour: 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3. Then work out the total time.

ch11.title: 💸 Salary and spending
ch11.description: You have spent 1/4 of your salary on rent, and 1/3 of what was left on food. If you still have €600, what was your salary?
ch11.hint: After the rent you have 3/4 left. Food is 1/3 × 3/4 = 1/4.
ch11.success: Perfect! Rent + Food = 1/2. So €600 is half of the salary. Total €1,200.
ch11.error: Be careful with the part of 'what was left'! 1/4 is the rent and 1/4 is the food.

ch12.title: 💀 The Final Challenge: The Water Tank
ch12.description: Three farmers share a water tank. The first uses 1/4, the second uses 1/3 of what is left, and the third uses 2/5 of the rest. If 1,800 litres are left, how many litres were there at the start?
ch12.hint: Work backwards: 1,800 L is 3/5 of what there was before the third farmer. Continue step by step back to the start.
ch12.success: Excellent! In the end, 3/4 × 2/3 × 3/5 = 3/10 of the water is left. If 3/10 is 1,800 L, there were 6,000 L at the start.
ch12.error: Step by step: Final = X × 3/4 × 2/3 × 3/5 = 1,800. Solve for X.

theory.title: Fractions Theory
theory.subtitle: Everything you need to know about fractions for 2nd ESO
theory.subtitle_dbh1: Everything you need to know about fractions for 1st ESO
theory.description: Explore each topic by clicking on the cards. The content will expand to show explanations, examples and tips for mastering fractions.

definition.title: Definition
definition.text1: A fraction is a mathematical expression that represents a part of a whole. It is made up of two numbers separated by a line:
definition.partWholeText: Represents a part of an object divided into equal parts.
definition.partWholeExample: Example: 2/3 of a pizza means 2 out of 3 equal parts.
definition.quotientText: Represents the division of two numbers.
definition.operatorText: Acts as a multiplier on an amount.
definition.ratioText: Compares two quantities of the same kind.
definition.tip: 💡 Tip: The denominator can never be zero (0), because you cannot divide by nothing.

types.title: Types according to the numerator and denominator
types.properExample: They represent less than one whole
types.improperExample: They represent more than one whole
types.unitExample: One part out of n equal parts
types.mixedText: Improper fractions can be converted into mixed numbers, which combine a whole-number part and a proper fraction.
types.tip: 💡 Tip: To convert a mixed number into an improper fraction: (whole number × denominator) + numerator, all over the same denominator.

equivalent.title: What are equivalent fractions?
equivalent.text1: Two fractions are equivalent when they represent the same amount, even though they have different numerators and denominators.
equivalent.propText: If we multiply or divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number (other than zero), we get an equivalent fraction.
equivalent.tip: 💡 Tip: To check whether two fractions are equivalent, cross-multiply: a×d must be equal to b×c.

compare.sameDenomTitle: Comparing fractions with the same denominator
compare.sameDenomText: If two fractions have the same denominator, the one with the larger numerator is the larger fraction.
compare.diffDenomText: First, we reduce them to a common denominator using the LCM (least common multiple) of the denominators.
compare.methodStep1: Calculate the LCM of the denominators
compare.methodStep2: Convert both fractions to that common denominator

addSubtract.sameDenomTitle: Adding and subtracting with the same denominator
addSubtract.sameDenomText: If the fractions have the same denominator, we add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator.
addSubtract.diffDenomTitle: Adding and subtracting with different denominators
addSubtract.diffDenomText: We reduce them to a common denominator using the LCM, then we do the same as before.
addSubtract.step1: Calculate the LCM of the denominators
addSubtract.step2: Convert both fractions to the LCM
addSubtract.warning: ⚠️ Common mistake: Never add the denominators. 1/2 + 1/2 ≠ 2/4, but 2/2 = 1

multiply.title: Multiplying fractions
multiply.text: To multiply fractions, we multiply numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator.
multiply.simplificationText: We can cross-simplify before multiplying, dividing one numerator and one denominator by their GCD.
multiply.fractionOfNumberText: Working out a fraction of an amount means multiplying the fraction by that amount.
multiply.tip: 💡 Tip: The word "of" between a fraction and a number means multiplication.

divide.title: Dividing fractions
divide.text: To divide fractions, we multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second.
divide.inverseTitle: What is the reciprocal of a fraction?
divide.inverseText: The reciprocal of a fraction is found by swapping the numerator and the denominator.
divide.integerText: We turn the integer into a fraction (by writing 1 as the denominator) and apply the same rule.
divide.tip: 💡 Remember: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. Never divide numerators and denominators directly!

powers.title: Powers of fractions
powers.text: To raise a fraction to a power, we raise both the numerator and the denominator to that power.
powers.negativeText: A negative exponent means we take the reciprocal of the fraction and raise it to the positive power.
powers.tip: 💡 Tip: Any fraction raised to 0 is equal to 1: (a/b)⁰ = 1

combined.title: Order of operations
combined.text: When there are several operations, we follow the order of priority:
combined.priority3: Multiplications and divisions (from left to right)
combined.priority4: Additions and subtractions (from left to right)
combined.warning: ⚠️ Common mistake: Not working from left to right when operations are at the same level. Multiplication and division have the same priority!
combined.tip: 💡 Tip: If you are not sure, use brackets to make the order clear. It is better to add too many than to get it wrong!

decimals.fracToDecText: To convert a fraction to a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator.
decimals.methodPower10: Scale up to a power of 10
decimals.typeExactDesc: They have a finite number of decimal places
decimals.typeExactCond: The denominator only has factors of 2 and/or 5
decimals.typePureDesc: A group of decimal digits repeats forever
decimals.typePureCond: The denominator has no factors of 2 or 5
decimals.typeMixedDesc: There are non-recurring decimals, followed by recurring ones
decimals.typeMixedCond: The denominator has factors of 2 or 5 and others
decimals.stepExact1: Numerator: the number without the decimal point
decimals.stepExact2: Denominator: 1 followed by as many zeros as there are decimal places
decimals.stepPure2: Denominator: as many 9s as there are digits in the repeating part
decimals.stepMixed2: Denominator: as many 9s as there are digits in the repeating part, followed by as many 0s as there are non-recurring decimal places
decimals.tip: 💡 Tip: If the decimal is greater than 1, separate the whole-number part, convert only the decimal part, then add them together.

proportionality.title: Ratio and proportion
proportionality.text: A ratio is the quotient of two amounts. A proportion is an equality between two ratios.
proportionality.directText: If one increases, the other increases by the same proportion.
proportionality.inverseText: If one increases, the other decreases by the same proportion.
proportionality.ruleOfThreeText: A method for solving proportionality problems.
proportionality.problem: Problem: If 3 kg of apples cost €6, how much do 5 kg cost?
proportionality.tip: 💡 Tip: Multiply across and divide by the leftover value: (value sought × cross value) ÷ value beside it

percentages.title: What is a percentage?
percentages.text: A percentage is a fraction with a denominator of 100. It is shown with the % symbol.
percentages.calcTitle: Working out a percentage of an amount
percentages.calcText: We multiply the amount by the percentage written as a fraction.
percentages.tip:
💡 Quick tip:
• 10% = divide by 10
• 20% = divide by 5
• 25% = divide by 4
• 50% = divide by 2
• 75% = divide by 4 and multiply by 3

home.description: Discover the hidden rules of numbers. Learn to find multiples, divisors, LCM and GCD, essential tools for simplifying problems.

f1.title: Multiples and Divisors
f1.desc: Understand the basic relationship between numbers.

f2.desc: Learn quick tricks to tell whether one number is divisible by another.

f3.title: Prime Numbers
f3.desc: Discover the 'building blocks' of all numbers.

curriculum.title: Curriculum Alignment for 1st ESO
curriculum.c1: Identifying multiples and divisors of a number.
curriculum.c4: Calculating and applying the LCM and GCD to solve problems.

conceptos.title: Multiples and Divisors
conceptos.subtitle: The basic relationship
conceptos.description: Understanding how numbers relate through multiplication and exact division.

multiplos.title: Multiples of a number
multiplos.text: The multiples of a number are all the possible results of multiplying that number by each natural number.

divisores.title: Divisors of a number
divisores.text: The divisors of a number are the numbers that can divide it an exact number of times, that is, with no remainder.

criterios.title: Quick Divisibility Rules
criterios.subtitle: Mathematical shortcuts
criterios.description: There are simple rules that let us tell whether a number is divisible by another without doing the division.

primos.title: Prime and Composite Numbers
primos.subtitle: The building blocks
primos.description: Sorting numbers by how many divisors they have.

primos.title: Prime Numbers
primos.text: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has only two different divisors: itself and 1.

compuestos.title: Composite Numbers
compuestos.text: A composite number is any natural number greater than 1 that is not prime. That is, it has more than two divisors.

descomposicion.title: Prime Factorisation
descomposicion.text: Any composite number can be written as a unique product of prime numbers. This process is called prime factorisation.

mcmMcd.title: LCM and GCD
mcmMcd.subtitle: Common multiples and divisors
mcmMcd.description: How to find the least common multiple and the greatest common divisor using factorisation.

mcm.title: Least Common Multiple (LCM)
mcm.text: The smallest number that is a multiple of all the numbers in the group. Rule: take all the prime factors (common and non-common), each raised to its highest exponent.

mcd.title: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)
mcd.text: The largest number that can divide all the numbers in the group without leaving a remainder. Rule: take only the common prime factors, each raised to its lowest exponent.

divisorChecker.title: Check Divisibility
divisorChecker.desc: Check whether one number is divisible by another

lcmGcd.title: LCM and GCD Calculator
lcmGcd.desc: Calculate the least common multiple and greatest common divisor

rules.title: Divisibility Rules
rules.desc: Check which divisibility rules a number satisfies
rules.rule3: The sum of its digits is a multiple of 3
rules.rule9: The sum of its digits is a multiple of 9
rules.rule11: The difference between the sums of the digits in even and odd positions is 0 or a multiple of 11

home.title: Natural Numbers
home.subtitle: Operations, mental calculation and order of operations
home.description: Learn the basic concepts of natural numbers, develop mental calculation strategies and master the order of operations.

theory.title: Natural and Decimal Numbers
theory.subtitle: Discover the Number Line and the Operations
theory.description: Learn how to use natural and decimal numbers, together with the D-P-E method for solving problems.

mentalMath.title: Mental Calculation Strategies
mentalMath.subtitle: Techniques for Calculating Faster
mentalMath.description: Mental calculation means doing mathematical operations without a calculator or other tools. Developing this skill will give you speed and a better understanding of numbers.

rounding.title: Round and Adjust
rounding.text: Round one of the numbers to the nearest ten or hundred, do the operation, then adjust the result.

breakdown.title: Break Down
breakdown.text: Split one of the numbers into easier parts.

order.title: Order of Operations
order.subtitle: Hierarchy of Operations
order.description: When an expression has more than one operation, we must follow a specific order to make sure everyone gets the same result.
order.rule1: Brackets: First, work out the operations inside the brackets.
order.rule2: Multiplication and Division: Work from left to right.
order.rule3: Addition and Subtraction: Work these out last, from left to right.
order.exampleText:
9 - (1 + 3) · 2
= 9 - 4 · 2    // First we work out what is inside the brackets so that we can subtract
= 9 - 8        // Next we do the multiplication
= 1            // Finally we do the subtraction

ops.title: Basic Operations
ops.subtitle: Definition and Properties
ops.description: Natural numbers are used for counting and ordering. The main operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

addition.title: Addition
addition.text: It means putting quantities together. The result is the same whatever order the numbers are added in (commutative property).

subtraction.title: Subtraction
subtraction.text: It means taking one quantity away from another. Careful! It is not commutative.

multiplication.title: Multiplication
multiplication.text: It is a short way of adding the same number several times. It has the commutative property.

division.title: Division
division.text: It means sharing a quantity into equal parts.

pdfTheory.title: Natural and Decimal Numbers
pdfTheory.subtitle: Discover the Number Line and Operations
pdfTheory.description: Learn to use natural and decimal numbers, together with the D-P-E method for solving problems.

arruntak.title: Natural Numbers
arruntak.description: We use natural numbers (0, 1, 2, 3...) to represent whole quantities.

segidak.title: Sequences and Number Line
segidak.text: If we have two known numbers on a number line, calculate the distance between them and divide by the number of intervals.

biribiltzea.title: Rounding to Thousands
biribiltzea.text: If the digit on the right is 5 or more, add one. If it is 4 or less, leave it as it is.

eragiketak.title: Combined Operations
eragiketak.text: Order of operations: 1. Brackets, 2. Multiplication and division, 3. Addition and subtraction.

hamartarrak.title: Decimal Numbers
hamartarrak.description: Decimals are used to represent parts smaller than one unit.

zuzena.title: Placing on the Number Line
zuzena.text: Always add a zero at the end (e.g. 9.7 -> 9.70) to see it more clearly.

biribiltzea.title: Rounding to Tenths
biribiltzea.text: If the hundredths digit is 5 or more, add one to the tenths digit.

eragiketak.title: Calculation Method
eragiketak.text: Addition/Subtraction: line up all the decimal points in the same column. Multiplication/Division (10, 100, 1000): move the decimal point as many places as there are zeros, to the right or to the left.

dpe.title: D-P-E Method for Solving Problems
dpe.description: To solve a problem correctly, you must always follow this structure:

datuak.title: D - Data
datuak.text: Read the text and pick out only the necessary mathematical information. Only keywords and numbers.

prozedura.title: P - Procedure
prozedura.text: Write the mathematical set-up clearly. If possible, do it in one single combined operation.

erantzuna.title: E - Answer
erantzuna.text: Never leave a number on its own. Always answer with a complete sentence.

semaforo.title: The Traffic Light for Combined Operations
semaforo.text: Red: brackets. Yellow: multiplication/division. Green: addition/subtraction.

dirua.title: Decimals vs. Cents
dirua.text: If you have trouble with decimals, think in euros and cents. The brain processes money better.

rol.title: Role-Play Game
rol.text: Do a calculation with a deliberate mistake, then try to spot that mistake and explain why.

ch1.title: 📌 Placing on the Number Line
ch1.description: On a number line, the interval between 5,000 and 6,000 is divided into four parts. Which number is at the first mark?
ch1.error: Find the length of each interval by dividing the total span (1000) by 4.

ch2.title: 🔄 Rounding
ch2.success: Correct! As the hundreds digit is 4 (< 5), the thousands digit stays the same: 26,000.
ch2.error: Look at the digit to the right of the thousands digit (4).

ch3.title: 🚦 The Traffic Light
ch3.error: First do the multiplications and divisions. Then add and subtract from left to right.

ch4.title: 🎯 Tenths
ch4.success: Correct! The hundredths digit is 6, which is greater than 5, so we add 1 to the tenths digit: 14.7.
ch4.error: Look at the digit to the right of the tenths digit (6).

ch5.title: ✖️ Quick Multiplication
ch5.description: What is the result of doing this multiplication in your head? 7.5 × 1000.
ch5.success: Great! The decimal point moves 3 places to the right: 7,500.
ch5.error: Move the decimal point to the right according to the number of zeros.

ch6.title: ➖ Aligned Subtraction
ch6.description: What is the result of this subtraction (remember to line up the decimal points): 15.73 - 9.98?
ch6.success: Excellent! By lining up the decimal points correctly and paying attention to the carries, the result is 5.75.
ch6.error: Line up the decimal points vertically and do a normal subtraction.

ch7.title: 📏 D-P-E Procedure
ch7.description: A building has 27 floors. Each floor has 12 flats, and each flat has 7 windows. What is the correct PROCEDURE for calculating the windows?
ch7.success: Correct! As all the relationships are multiplicative, the procedure is 27 × 12 × 7.
ch7.error: When some items appear repeatedly within a quantity of other items, you multiply.

ch8.title: 📊 D-P-E Data
ch8.description: I have €50 and I want to buy an item of clothing for €32.89 and a ball for €17.50. What should be written in the DATA section?
options: All of the text, word for word.
ch8.success: Of course! In the data, only the important information should be written, without calculations.
ch8.error: The data should not include calculations, only a useful summary of the problem.

ch9.title: ✍️ D-P-E Answer
ch9.description: When you have the numerical result of the previous problem (0.39 is missing), how should the ANSWER section be written?
options: 'I'm short of money, I'm missing exactly €0.39.'
ch9.success: Well done! E (Answer) must always be written as a complete sentence, to give context.
ch9.error: Answers are not just numbers on their own; they always need an explanatory sentence.

f1.title: The Set ℤ

f2.title: Absolute Value

f3.title: Addition and Subtraction

f4.title: Advanced Operations

curriculum.title: Curriculum Alignment: 1st ESO
curriculum.c1: Identifying and using integers in real-life contexts (temperatures, debts).
curriculum.c2: Representing and ordering numbers on the number line.

curriculum.c4: Basic and combined operations with integers, following the order of operations.

theory.title: Integers Theory
theory.subtitle: Discover the set ℤ
theory.description: Learn how to use positive and negative numbers to solve everyday and mathematical problems.

concepto.title: The Set ℤ and the Number Line
concepto.description: Integers include the natural numbers (positive ones), their opposites (negative ones) and zero. They are used to represent debts, temperatures below zero or depths.

recta.title: The Number Line
recta.text: Zero is the origin. Positive numbers (>0) are on the right and negative numbers (<0) are on the left.

absoluto.title: Absolute Value
absoluto.text: It is the distance of a number from zero. It is always positive or zero. It is written between bars | |.

operaciones.title: Addition and Subtraction
operaciones.description: Think of addition and subtraction as movements on the number line: adding a positive number is moving forward (to the right), and adding a negative number is moving back (to the left).

sumaMismo.title: Adding numbers with the same sign
sumaMismo.text: Add their absolute values and keep the sign.

sumaDiferente.title: Adding numbers with different signs
sumaDiferente.text: Subtract their absolute values and use the sign of the number with the larger absolute value.

resta.title: Subtraction
resta.text: Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite.

avanzadas.title: Advanced Operations
avanzadas.description: Rules for multiplication, division and combined operations.

multDiv.title: Multiplication and Division
multDiv.text:
Apply the Rule of Signs:
• Same signs: positive result (+)
• Different signs: negative result (-)

combinadas.title: Combined Operations
combinadas.text: Follow the same order of operations as with natural numbers, paying attention to the signs.

lab.title: Integers Lab
lab.subtitle: Interactive calculator for practising with integers.

integerCalculator.title: Special Calculator
integerCalculator.desc: Try additions, subtractions, multiplications and divisions with negative numbers.

algebra.title: Algebra
algebra.subtitle: The magic of mental calculation: letters and equations

theory.description: Learn the basics of algebra, expressions and equations.

letras.title: 1. Letters and Expressions
letras.p1: In situations where we do not know an exact value, we use a letter to represent it. We call this letter an <1>unknown</1> or a <3>variable</3>. This lets us generalise rules and solve complex problems.
letras.example1: <0>Example:</0> If Juan's age is 'x', in 15 years he will be 'x + 15' years old, and a year ago he was 'x - 1'.
letras.p2: An algebraic expression is a combination of numbers, letters (variables) and mathematical operations.
letras.c1: <0>Letters (variables):</0> They represent unknown values (x, y, a, b...).
letras.c2: <0>Numbers (coefficients):</0> The known values that multiply the variables.
letras.example2: <0>Examples:</0> 3x - 5 (three times a number minus five), x² + 1 (the square of a number plus one).

ecuaciones.title: 2. Equations
ecuaciones.p1: An equation is an equality between two algebraic expressions that contains one or more unknown values (unknowns). It is like a balanced scale: what is on one side of the equals sign (=) must be worth the same as what is on the other side.
ecuaciones.goal: <0>The goal:</0> To find the value of the unknown (usually 'x') that makes the equation true.
ecuaciones.p2: To solve a first-degree equation, we follow some steps to 'solve for x', that is, to leave x on its own on one side of the equals sign.
ecuaciones.step1_desc: We move all the terms that have the unknown (x) to one side of the equals sign, and all the numbers to the other side. <1>Key rule:</1> whatever is added on one side moves to the other side as a subtraction, and vice versa.
ecuaciones.step2_desc: We work on each side of the equals sign to simplify the expression.
ecuaciones.step3_desc: If the 'x' has a coefficient (a number multiplying it), we move it to the other side by dividing.
ecuaciones.p3: The real power of algebra is translating real-life problems into mathematical language that we can solve.
ecuaciones.problem_example:
<0>Problem: A pile of coins and one seventh of that pile add up to 24 euros. How much is the pile worth?

<3>Setting up: x + (1/7)x = 24

<6>Solution: (8/7)x = 24 → x = (24 × 7) / 8 → x = 21. The pile is worth 21 euros.

monomios.title: 3. Operations with Monomials
monomios.p1: Only <1>like</1> monomials can be added or subtracted, that is, those with the same literal part (the same letters with the same exponents).
monomios.rule_desc: Add or subtract the coefficients and keep the same literal part.
monomios.p2: To multiply or divide monomials, work with the coefficients and the literal parts separately.
monomios.mult_desc: Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents of the same letters.
monomios.div_desc: Divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents of the same letters.
monomios.dist_desc: When a monomial multiplies a sum or subtraction, it multiplies each of the terms.

lab.title: Equations Lab
lab.subtitle: Solve equations automatically and practise algebra.

geometria.title: Geometry
geometria.subtitle: The study of shapes and space

theory.description: Learn about triangles, quadrilaterals and their properties. Discover Pythagoras' theorem and learn how to calculate areas and perimeters.

lab.description: Use our interactive tools to work with different geometric shapes and test your knowledge.

triangles.title: Triangles
triangles.intro: Triangles are polygons that have three sides and three angles.

isosceles.name: Isosceles
isosceles.desc: It has two equal sides and one different side.

acute.name: Acute
acute.desc: All three angles are acute (less than 90°).

right.name: Right-angled
right.desc: It has one right angle (equal to 90°).

obtuse.name: Obtuse
obtuse.desc: It has one obtuse angle (greater than 90°).

parallelograms.title: Parallelograms
parallelograms.desc: Their opposite sides are parallel in pairs.

rectangle.name: Rectangle
rectangle.desc: Opposite sides are equal, and there are 4 right angles.

rhombus.name: Rhombus
rhombus.desc: 4 equal sides and equal opposite angles.

rhomboid.name: Rhomboid
rhomboid.desc: Opposite sides and opposite angles are equal.

trapezium.name: Trapezium
trapezium.desc: Only two of its opposite sides are parallel.

trapezoid.name: Trapezoid
trapezoid.desc: No side is parallel to its opposite side.

pythagoras.title: Pythagoras' Theorem
pythagoras.desc: In every right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the legs.
pythagoras.legend: Where 'c' is the hypotenuse, and 'a' and 'b' are the legs.

areas_perimeters.title: Areas and Perimeters
areas_perimeters.desc: Formulas for calculating the area and perimeter of the most common plane shapes.

lab.title: Geometry Room
lab.subtitle: Calculate the area of random shapes.
lab.find_area: Calculate the area of this shape.
lab.find_area_rounded: Calculate the area of this shape (rounded to the nearest integer).
lab.incorrect: Incorrect. Try again or look at the solution.

home.title: Tables and Graphs
home.subtitle: Represent the world of data
home.description: Learn how to collect, organise and represent information using statistics.

f1.title: Population and Sample
f1.desc: Learn who to ask to get information.

f2.title: Statistical Variables
f2.desc: Learn to tell the difference between types of data (qualitative and quantitative).

f3.title: Frequencies and Tables
f3.desc: Learn how to organise data and understand what it means.

f4.title: Graphs and Measures
f4.desc: Learn to create graphs and analyse basic statistical measures (Mean, Median, Mode).

curriculum.title: Curriculum Alignment: 1st ESO
curriculum.c1: Understanding the concepts of population, sample and individual.
curriculum.c2: Telling apart qualitative and quantitative statistical variables.
curriculum.c3: Creating absolute and relative frequency tables.
curriculum.c4: Representing data using bar charts and pie charts.

poblacion.title: Population and Sample
poblacion.description: Before collecting information, we must be clear about who we are going to ask.

population.title: Population
population.text: It is the set of ALL the elements or people that we want to study.

sample.title: Sample
sample.text: It is a representative part of the population. We often cannot ask everyone, so we take a sample.

individual.title: Individual
individual.text: Each one of the members of the population or sample.

variables.title: Statistical Variables
variables.description: It is the characteristic that is studied for each individual.

qualitative.title: Qualitative Variables
qualitative.text: They are not measured with numbers. They represent a quality or characteristic (e.g. eye colour, favourite sport).

quantitative.title: Quantitative Variables
quantitative.text: They are expressed using numbers. They can be of two types:
quantitative.discrete: Discrete: They take separate values, usually integers (e.g. number of siblings: 0, 1, 2...).
quantitative.continuous: Continuous: They can take any value within an interval, including decimals (e.g. height, weight).

frecuencias.title: Frequencies and Tables
frecuencias.description: We organise data into tables to understand it better.

absolute.title: Absolute Frequency (fi)
absolute.text: The number of times a value or piece of data appears.

relative.title: Relative Frequency (hi)
relative.text: It is the result of dividing the absolute frequency by the total number of data (N): hi = fi / N.

percentage.title: Percentage (%)
percentage.text: It is found by multiplying the relative frequency by 100. It shows what percentage of the total it represents.

graficos.title: Statistical Graphs
graficos.description: They are used to understand data visually and quickly.

bar.title: Bar Chart
bar.text: It is used for qualitative or discrete quantitative variables. The frequency is shown by the height of the bars.

pie.title: Pie Chart
pie.text: Ideal for showing the parts (percentages) of a total. The circle is divided into slices, like a pie.

medidas.title: Statistical Measures
medidas.description: To summarise a set of data with one or a few values.

media.title: Arithmetic Mean
media.text: The sum of all the data divided by the number of data values. (Only possible with quantitative variables.)

mediana.title: Median
mediana.text: The value in the middle after the data are put in order from smallest to largest.

moda.title: Mode
moda.text: The value that appears most often (the one with the highest absolute frequency).

rango.title: Range
rango.text: The difference between the maximum value and the minimum value.

variablesTool.title: Classify the Variables
variablesTool.description: Choose the correct type for each element.

frequencyTool.title: Complete the Table
frequencyTool.description: Calculate the relative frequency and the percentage from this data.
frequencyTool.incorrect: There are mistakes in the table. Review it.
